subject: physics
title: Electromagnetic induction
key_idea: A changing magnetic flux linkage induces an e.m.f. Faraday's law gives its size, ε = −Δ(NΦ)/Δt, and Lenz's law gives its direction: it opposes the change that causes it.

blocks.text: Flux measures how much magnetic field passes through an area. Only the part of the field at right angles to the area counts.

items.meaning: The product of the magnetic flux density and the area at right angles to it.
The unit of flux. 1 Wb = 1 T m².
The flux multiplied by the number of turns N of the coil that it passes through.

blocks.label: Magnetic flux
where: θ = angle between the field and the normal (the line at right angles) to the coil

blocks.label: Flux linkage
where: N = number of turns on the coil

items: When the field is at right angles to the coil's face, θ = 0 and the flux is BA, the greatest value.
When the field is parallel to the face of the coil, θ = 90° and the flux is zero.
So rotating a coil in a field makes the flux linkage change.
Φ = BA cos θ, measured in webers.
Flux linkage is NΦ, the flux times the number of turns.

blocks.text: Changing the flux linkage induces an e.m.f. Two laws give its size and its direction.

items.meaning: The magnitude of the induced e.m.f. is equal to the rate of change of flux linkage.
The induced e.m.f. is in a direction that opposes the change that produces it.

blocks.label: Induced e.m.f.
where: Δt = time taken for the change (s)

items: The minus sign shows Lenz's law: the e.m.f. opposes the change.
In calculus form, ε = −d(NΦ)/dt. This is the gradient of a graph of flux linkage against time.
If the circuit is complete, the e.m.f. drives a current.
An induced current that helped the change would make the change bigger, which would make more current, and so on. Energy would be created from nothing.
Instead, work is done against the opposing force, such as pushing a magnet into a coil.
That work is transferred to electrical energy in the circuit.

diagram.alt: A prediction activity. Choose what the magnet does and see which pole the coil makes at the end nearest the magnet, and the force on the magnet.
diagram.prompt: A bar magnet moves near one end of a coil connected to a closed circuit. What does it do?
result_labels: Pole induced at the end of the coil nearest the magnet

options.label: North pole moves towards the coil
results: The flux linkage is increasing, so the coil makes a field to push the magnet back

options.label: North pole moves away from the coil
results: The flux linkage is decreasing, so the coil makes a field to hold the magnet back

options.label: South pole moves towards the coil
results: The flux linkage is increasing, so the coil makes a field to push the magnet back

options.label: South pole moves away from the coil
results: The flux linkage is decreasing, so the coil makes a field to hold the magnet back

items: Size of e.m.f. = rate of change of flux linkage.
Direction: the induced current opposes the change causing it. This is conservation of energy.

blocks.text: Moving a magnet into a coil connected to a sensitive voltmeter shows the effects.

items: An e.m.f. is induced only while the magnet is moving, that is, while the flux linkage is changing. A stationary magnet gives none.
Pushing the magnet in or pulling it out gives e.m.f.s of opposite sign.
Reversing the magnet gives the opposite sign again.
Moving the magnet faster, which makes the rate of change of flux larger.
A stronger magnet, which makes B larger.
More turns on the coil, which makes N larger.
A coil with a larger area.

diagram.alt: A slider activity. A magnetic field through a coil is reduced to zero. Change the number of turns, the flux density, the area and the time taken and see the average induced e.m.f.

inputs.label: Time taken to remove the field

items: A changing flux linkage induces an e.m.f. A steady one does not.
The e.m.f. is larger for a faster change, a stronger field, more turns or a larger area.

sections.heading: Investigating flux with a search coil

blocks.text: A search coil is a small coil of many turns. It samples the flux in a region by the e.m.f. induced in it.

items.text: Place the search coil in the changing field of a coil connected to an a.c. supply.
Connect the search coil to an oscilloscope. Read the peak value of the induced e.m.f.
Turn the search coil in steps of about 10° and record the peak e.m.f. each time.
Graph the peak e.m.f. against the angle θ between the coil's axis and the field.

items: The peak e.m.f. is greatest when the axis of the search coil is along the field (θ = 0).
It is zero when the axis is at right angles to the field (θ = 90°).
The graph follows cos θ, because the flux linkage is BAN cos θ.
The e.m.f. in a search coil is proportional to the rate of change of flux linkage.
It varies as cos θ as the coil is rotated.

checks.q: A coil of 200 turns and area 4.0 × 10⁻³ m² is at right angles to a field of flux density 0.30 T. Calculate the flux linkage.
The field in the previous coil falls uniformly to zero in 0.050 s. Calculate the average e.m.f. induced.
Explain how Lenz's law is an example of the conservation of energy.
checks.a: The induced current opposes the change that causes it, for example by exerting a force on a moving magnet. Work has to be done against this force and the work is transferred into electrical energy. If the current helped the motion, energy would be created from nothing.

blocks.text: A straight conductor moving in a field

items.text: A conductor of length l moves at speed v at right angles to a field B. In time Δt it sweeps an area lvΔt.
The flux cut is ΔΦ = B l v Δt.
ε = ΔΦ/Δt = Blv, for one conductor (N = 1).

blocks.text: A coil rotating in a field

items.text: A coil rotating at constant angular speed ω has θ = ωt.

items: The peak e.m.f. is BANω, when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field and the sides cut the field fastest.
The e.m.f. is zero when the plane of the coil is at right angles to the field.
The e.m.f. is sinusoidal, with frequency f = ω/2π.
Straight conductor: ε = Blv.
Rotating coil: ε = BANω sin ωt.

blocks.text: A changing current in a linked coil
A coil carrying a current makes a magnetic field. If its current changes, the flux through a second coil linked with it changes too.

items: The changing flux linkage in the second coil induces an e.m.f. in it.
A constant current in the first coil induces no e.m.f.
A faster change of current gives a larger e.m.f.
More turns on the second coil, or a coil that shares more of the flux (such as one wound on the same iron core), gives a larger e.m.f.
Lenz's law gives the direction: it opposes the change of flux.
A changing current in one coil induces an e.m.f. in a linked coil.
The e.m.f. depends on how fast the current changes and how well the coils are linked.
